summary: Argues that standards bodies working on protocols of mutual interest without formal coordination can cause serious problems, some of which may harm the Internet. It suggests that a robust process for joint development is needed. It is an informational IAB document.

eli5.summary: If two teams build parts of the same bridge without talking, the pieces may not fit. This document warns that standards groups need to work together so the Internet does not suffer.

questions: why is uncoordinated protocol development harmful
what is the t-mpls case study
subtitle: Why standards bodies must coordinate when developing shared protocols.

tldr.problem: When different standards development organizations (SDOs) like the IETF and ITU-T work independently on protocols that affect the same network, they may make incompatible changes that break the Internet or create serious interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC uses the Transport MPLS (T-MPLS) case study to show how uncoordinated protocol modification violates fundamental design principles: it redefines protocol invariants, changes code-point semantics, and assumes that incompatible variants can coexist ('ships in the night') even though they share the same identifying numbers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends that SDOs establish formal coordination procedures and that one organization maintain design authority for each protocol. The IETF and ITU-T resolved the T-MPLS conflict by creating a joint team (JWT) to develop MPLS-TP, a coordinated solution that satisfies both transport network and Internet protocol needs.

today: RFC 5704 is an Informational RFC published in November 2009 by the Internet Architecture Board. It remains relevant as standards bodies continue to develop overlapping protocols. The IETF and ITU-T have improved their coordination through the mechanisms described in this RFC, though the fundamental lesson—that uncoordinated protocol development risks harm to the Internet—applies to all standards organizations.

sections.title: Why Standards Bodies Must Talk
sections.content:
The Internet has become critical infrastructure for global commerce and communications. Because the Internet is so important and so large, a protocol failure can cause massive, widespread damage. Many Internet protocols are developed by different standards groups: the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) controls Internet protocols like TCP and IP, while the ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunication Standardization Sector) develops telephone and telecom standards.

Problems emerge when these groups work independently on protocols that overlap. If ITU-T designs a new version of MPLS without consulting IETF (which created MPLS), they may make changes that break IETF's design, causing equipment incompatibility and network failures. This RFC uses real examples to show why coordination is essential and how the IETF and ITU-T learned to work together.
sections.eli5: Imagine two teams building a bridge from opposite sides without measuring—the halves might not meet. Internet standards groups need to measure together before building new protocols.

sections.title: Protocol Design Principles
sections.content:
Protocol designers rely on certain invariants: fixed properties that remain true across the entire Internet. For example, the Time To Live (TTL) field in IP decreases by 1 at each hop and stops forwarding when it reaches zero. This invariant prevents packets from looping forever if routing goes wrong. Another invariant is the MPLS reserved label numbers 0 to 15, which have special meanings; higher numbers can be freely allocated by routers.

A code-point is a number or identifier that tells a packet processor what to do with a packet. Once a code-point is assigned (such as MPLS Label 14), its meaning must never change. If a new use case requires different behavior, a new code-point must be obtained, not the old one redefined. This is because equipment worldwide has been built with the assumption that Label 14 always means the same thing.

Each protocol must have a single design authority: the organization responsible for deciding what that protocol is and how it evolves. IETF is the design authority for MPLS and IP. Once designed authority is established, other groups must ask permission before making changes. Some designers argue protocols can coexist in 'ships in the night'—operating in separate networks and never meeting. This RFC shows why that assumption is false: networks inevitably overlap, and equipment cannot tell which variant it has received.
sections.eli5: A protocol is like a rulebook for talking on the Internet. Once you say that red means 'stop,' you can never change it to 'go' because everyone has already learned red means 'stop.' All rule changes must go through the original author (the design authority) to keep everyone on the same page.

sections.title: Case Study: Transport MPLS (T-MPLS)
sections.content:
In the 2000s, ITU-T wanted to design a protocol for transport networks (the high-speed backbone systems that telephone companies operate). ITU-T chose to build on MPLS, IETF's already-proven protocol for routing packets. However, ITU-T developed Transport MPLS (T-MPLS) largely without consulting IETF.

The Label 14 Problem: T-MPLS reused MPLS Reserved Label 14, which IETF had already assigned to a specific OAM (Operation and Maintenance) function. ITU-T defined a different behavior for Label 14. Now, if a packet marked with Label 14 traveled through both IETF MPLS and T-MPLS equipment, each type of router would interpret it differently, causing the packet to be handled incorrectly.

The TTL Problem: IETF MPLS follows the same TTL invariant as IP: TTL decreases at every hop and stops forwarding at zero. T-MPLS designers wanted to increase TTL at some hops to reach deeper OAM targets. This violated the MPLS architecture and could allow packets to loop forever under fault conditions.

The EXP Field Problem: The 3-bit EXP field in MPLS was reserved for future use but was intended for Quality of Service marking. T-MPLS redefined these bits for a different purpose (maintenance levels), conflicting with deployed hardware.

These changes, made without IETF coordination, would have created a parallel incompatible version of MPLS. Equipment built to IETF's MPLS could not safely interoperate with T-MPLS equipment, and networks using both would fail.
sections.eli5: ITU-T built T-MPLS by taking MPLS and changing the rules on three important things, without asking IETF first. It's like one team deciding their red means 'stop' while another team says red means 'go.' When both types of equipment are in the same network, packets get lost or misrouted.

sections.title: Another Example: PPP over SONET
sections.content:
IETF's RFC 1619 defined how to carry PPP (a protocol for connecting to Internet service providers) over SONET (Synchronous Optical Network), a standard for high-speed telecommunications links. RFC 1619 incorrectly stated that no scrambling was needed when inserting data into the SONET frame. Scrambling randomizes data to avoid patterns that confuse optical equipment.

ITU-T and ANSI (American National Standards Institute), the authorities on SONET, later found that this was wrong: SONET requires scrambling. Data sent without scrambling gets corrupted. This broke both routing and user data traffic on networks using RFC 1619.

This failure happened because IETF developed RFC 1619 without consulting SONET experts. The fix required publishing RFC 2615 with corrections and coordinating with the SONET experts—a slow and costly process. If IETF had worked with ITU-T and ANSI from the start, the error would never have occurred.
sections.eli5: IETF wrote the rules for sending Internet traffic over telephone backbone cables but forgot to ask the telephone experts. They got a critical rule wrong, broke the cables, and had to fix it later with the telephone experts' help.

sections.title: Learning to Coordinate: MPLS-TP
sections.content:
After the T-MPLS disaster became clear, the IETF and ITU-T recognized they needed a better approach. They created a Joint Working Team (JWT) to assess whether MPLS could be enhanced to meet transport network needs without breaking IETF's protocol architecture.

The JWT concluded that yes, MPLS could be safely extended. This led to MPLS-TP (MPLS Transport Profile), a protocol developed jointly by both organizations. IETF experts worked in ITU-T committees, and ITU-T experts worked in IETF working groups. ITU-T Recommendations now reference IETF RFCs for the technical definitions, avoiding duplication and conflicting definitions.

The RFC recommends two key improvements: (1) SDOs should confirm that all protocol changes are approved by the design authority before publishing, and (2) the IETF should define a universal change process (not just for MPLS) to make coordination clear and systematic. This way, future coordination can happen faster and cost less than the JWT effort.
sections.eli5: IETF and ITU-T decided to stop working separately. They made one joint team to design MPLS-TP together. Now ITU-T recommendations say 'see the IETF RFC for how this works,' so everyone gets the same rules.

sections.title: Why This Matters for Security
sections.content:
Uncoordinated protocol changes threaten both security and stability. When multiple incompatible versions of a protocol exist, network operators cannot predict how a packet will be handled, creating opportunities for attacks. An attacker might craft packets that one version processes in a dangerous way or that cause loops or disconnections.

Because MPLS and IP are fundamental to Internet infrastructure, modifying them carelessly increases the attack surface and risks widespread failure. IETF's security review process combines cross-area review with specialized expertise, preventing many common design errors. When changes are made outside this process, they bypass these safeguards. The RFC emphasizes that protocol security must be reviewed with special diligence when the protocol is core infrastructure like IP or MPLS.
sections.eli5: When packets don't know which version of a rule they should follow, attackers can exploit the confusion. And if the broken protocol is something all Internet routers use, the whole Internet gets more fragile.
